The rendered canvas displays the visual destination of our application. The parent container ChatWorkspace.jsx hosts both parts. At the top sits the channel selector bar with button pills. Below it sits the active chat room card, displaying the live channel badge, the message composer input, and the send button.

To construct this architecture, we follow a top-down assembly pipeline: we start with the parent workspace container and then build each nested child inside it:

Step 1
First, we construct the parent container ChatWorkspace.jsx

We start our implementation at the top: the parent container ChatWorkspace.jsx.

We begin here because the parent defines the layout and dictates the shared state for the entire workspace. It decides which room is currently active and coordinates the child components without touching websockets directly:

ChatWorkspace.jsx

3 const [roomId, setRoomId] = useState('general');

Look at line 3: const [roomId, setRoomId] = useState('general') We declare state here because multiple child components need to coordinate around the active channel.

Now look at line 6: <ChannelSelector activeRoom={roomId} onSelect={setRoomId} /> We have not coded ChannelSelector yet. But right here in the parent, we establish its contract. The parent passes down the active room string for styling, and passes setRoomId so the child can report user selections. We will build that child next in step 2.

Now look at line 7: <ChatRoom roomId={roomId} /> Notice that we pass roomId as a prop. Notice also that the parent contains zero effect code and zero socket logic. If we put the websocket connection in ChatWorkspace, switching channels would force the entire workspace layout to re-render and re-initialize. By delegating roomId downward as a prop, we turn ChatRoom into an isolated reactive boundary. We will build that component in steps 3 and 4.

To recap this first step: the parent holds the shared state that child components need to coordinate, and leaves external socket synchronization to the child boundary.

Step 2
Next, we build the channel selector child ChannelSelector.jsx

In step 2, we fulfill the contract established by the parent: we build ChannelSelector.jsx.

This child component is responsible for the channel navigation pills at the top of the workspace:

ChannelSelector.jsx
1export default function ChannelSelector({ activeRoom, onSelect }) {
2 const rooms = ['general', 'politics', 'breaking'];
3 return (
4 <nav className="channel-bar">
5 {rooms.map((room) => (
6 <button key={room} className={room === activeRoom ? 'active' : ''} onClick={() => onSelect(room)}>#{room}</button>
ACTION:
Notifies parent to update active channel
7 ))}
8 </nav>
9 );
10}

Notice the function parameters: we destructure { activeRoom, onSelect } directly from props. That matches the contract we wrote in step 1. ChannelSelector owns zero local state. It relies entirely on its parent to provide the active channel name and the function to update it.

Look at the button click handler on line 6: onClick={() => onSelect(room)}

Where does onSelect come from? Look back at Step 1 in ChatWorkspace.jsx. The parent declared const [roomId, setRoomId] = useState('general') and then rendered: <ChannelSelector activeRoom={roomId} onSelect={setRoomId} />

Notice what happened: the parent handed its private updater function setRoomId to the child under the prop name onSelect. ChannelSelector does not own state, and it does not know what roomId is used for. It only holds a telephone line called onSelect.

When the reporter clicks a button, the native browser onClick fires and calls onSelect(room). Because onSelect points directly to setRoomId, that call immediately executes setRoomId('politics') back in ChatWorkspace.

This is standard inverse data flow: data flows down through props (activeRoom), and user actions flow up through callbacks (onSelect).

What would happen if ChannelSelector opened the websocket connection itself?

If you put the useEffect or socket connection inside ChannelSelector, the navigation buttons would be trapped managing network sockets, reconnection timers, and message buffers. Worse, the chat message area in ChatRoom would have no way to access that socket without messy prop-drilling or global state hacks. You would have buttons and network protocols tangled in a single file.

By separating them, ChannelSelector owns zero useState and zero useEffect. It is a pure presenter: given the same activeRoom string and onSelect callback, it will always render the exact same three buttons.

This separation gives you two concrete superpowers:

  1. If tomorrow you replace the button pills with a dropdown <select> menu, you touch zero lines of websocket code.
  2. If you swap the websocket protocol in ChatRoom for a mock test service, you touch zero lines of button code.

To recap this step: user interactions in ChannelSelector flow upward to ChatWorkspace through onSelect, changing the parent's roomId state.

Step 3
Then, we declare the reactive effect in ChatRoom.jsx

In step 3, we build the core reactive boundary: slice 1 of ChatRoom.jsx.

Think about what must happen when roomId changes. The component receives a new roomId prop. It must terminate the previous websocket connection. Then it must open a new connection to the new channel:

ChatRoom.jsx
1export default function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {
2 const [status, setStatus] = useState('disconnected');
3 useEffect(() => {
4 const connection = createConnection(roomId);
SETUP:
Instantiates socket for current roomId
5 connection.connect(() => setStatus('connected'));
6 return () => {
7 connection.disconnect();
CLEANUP:
Terminates socket before next setup or unmount
8 setStatus('disconnected');
9 };
10 }, [roomId]);
DEPENDENCY:
Triggers cleanup and re-setup whenever roomId changes

Look closely at the useEffect call on lines 3 to 10. Notice the dependency array on line 10: [roomId]. This tells React that the effect depends on the value of roomId. Whenever roomId changes between renders, React must re-synchronize the effect.

Now look at the body of the effect on lines 4 and 5. That is your setup function. It calls createConnection(roomId) and initiates the connection with connection.connect(). When the socket opens, it updates local state to 'connected'.

Now look at lines 6 to 9: return () => { connection.disconnect(); setStatus('disconnected'); }; That return statement is your cleanup function. It tells React how to stop synchronizing.

Here is the vital rule of effect execution. When roomId changes from "general" to "politics", React does not just run the setup code with "politics". First, React runs the cleanup function returned during the "general" render. That disconnects the old socket. Only after the old socket is closed does React run the setup code with "politics".

To recap this step: the effect pairs every setup with a cleanup, ensuring that changing roomId cleanly shuts down the old channel before opening the new one.

Step 4
Finally, we seal the chat interface and message composer

In step 4, we complete ChatRoom.jsx by adding the message composer interface and closing the component tag:

ChatRoom.jsx (continued)

14 <h3>Channel: #{roomId}</h3>
15 <span className={`status-badge ${status}`}>{status}</span>

Notice the header on lines 13 to 16. It renders the current channel name #{roomId} and a status badge showing whether the socket is 'connected' or 'disconnected'.

Now look at the message area on lines 17 and 18. It provides an input and a Send button. When the reporter types a message and submits it, the message travels across the currently active websocket connection.

Notice what happens when the user switches channels: ChatRoom never unmounts from the DOM. The card stays in place. The input box stays in place. But behind the scenes, React executed the cleanup function to close the previous socket and executed the setup function to connect to the new socket.

The <section> boundary seals this entire workflow. It isolates connection management from the rest of the application. The parent container ChatWorkspace never has to know how websockets work, and ChannelSelector never has to know how connections are cleaned up.

Let us recap the senior rule. An effect does not represent component mounting or unmounting. An effect represents an ongoing synchronization cycle. When dependencies change, React always runs the cleanup from the previous render before running the setup for the next render.

Lessons from the Experiment: Naive Expectation vs Reality

Developers familiar with traditional component lifecycles instinctively assume that an effect only runs its cleanup function when the component is removed from the screen. This naive expectation leads to severe bugs: when props or state change, developers expect the effect to update in place, leaving old subscriptions active and creating zombie listeners.

In our experiment, the ChatRoom component remained mounted continuously while the reporter switched channels from "general" to "politics". However, React still ran the cleanup function for "general" before running the setup function for "politics". If React waited until unmount to run cleanup, the application would maintain two open sockets simultaneously, receiving duplicate messages and wasting network bandwidth.

To see the architectural hierarchy and component relationships at a glance, examine how each component functions in direct relation to the others:

ChatWorkspace

The parent container orchestrates the newsroom workspace layout. It owns the active channel state (roomId). Notice it provides two things: the state and updater callback downward to ChannelSelector, and the reactive roomId prop to ChatRoom. It isolates the workspace from connection logic so switching channels never unmounts the view.

ChannelSelectoractiveRoom={roomId} onSelect={setRoomId}

This is the channel selection control. It receives the active channel string and the updater callback from the parent. Notice it renders clean button pills with zero knowledge of websockets or network protocols. When clicked, it notifies the parent to update the channel.

ChatRoomroomId={roomId}

This is the reactive effect boundary. It receives roomId as a reactive prop. Notice that when roomId changes, the component does not unmount. Instead, React executes the cleanup function from the previous render to close the old socket, and then runs the new setup function to open the new socket.

The Exact Synchronization Sequence: Cleanup Before Re-Setup

To understand why React executes cleanup before re-setup, we must trace the exact sequence of events during a dependency transition. A dependency change is not a simple function call; it is an orchestrated three-step sequence. Without understanding this sequence, developers are baffled by console logs showing cleanup running with old prop values while the screen already displays new prop values.

Consider what happens when the user clicks the # politics button while currently connected to # general. First, React updates the roomId state in ChatWorkspace and re-renders the component tree. Second, React commits the changes to the DOM: the screen now paints the new title "Channel: #politics". Third, before running the new effect, React calls the cleanup function returned during the previous render. That cleanup function closed over roomId = "general", so it disconnects cleanly from # general. Fourth, React runs the effect setup function for the current render. That setup function closes over roomId = "politics", connecting to the new channel. If setup ran before cleanup, both connections would exist concurrently, causing race conditions and state corruption.

What happens in React 19 development with Strict Mode? When your component first mounts in development, React intentionally mounts the component, runs setup, runs cleanup immediately, and then runs setup a second time. Why? To prove that your cleanup function completely undoes whatever your setup function did. If your cleanup function is missing or incomplete, the second setup exposes the bug immediately during development before it reaches production users.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does cleanup see the old prop value? Imagine you write a letter, place it inside an envelope, and seal it shut. Inside that envelope, you wrote: "Please lock door number ten." Ten minutes later, you move to room twenty. Does moving to room twenty magically rewrite the letter inside the sealed envelope? Of course not. The sealed envelope still says: "Please lock door number ten." In JavaScript, a cleanup function is like that sealed envelope: it is a closure. When React created the cleanup function during the first render, it captured the old prop value roomId = "general". When React opens that envelope during the next render, it executes the instructions inside: it disconnects from "general", not "politics". This closure capture guarantees that cleanup always cleans up the exact resource that was opened.

Where you will meet this

  • Editorial websocket channels: Subscribing to live newsroom dispatches and disconnecting the old channel before opening the new one when reporters switch topics.
  • Document title and event observers: Attaching window resize or scroll listeners that re-bind to new target containers when layout dimensions change.
  • Real-time stock and score tickers: Subscribing to high-frequency market tickers where changing the selected asset requires terminating the previous data feed.
  • Video and audio player instances: Initializing native media player instances that must destroy existing playback sessions before mounting a new media stream.

Glossary

  • Reactive Effect: An effect declared with useEffect that synchronizes an external system with current props and state, re-running whenever its declared dependencies change.
  • Effect Lifecycle: The independent lifecycle of an effect, consisting solely of starting synchronization via setup and stopping synchronization via cleanup, distinct from component mounting.
  • Cleanup Function: A callback returned by an effect setup function that releases resources, cancels subscriptions, and disconnects sockets created during that synchronization cycle.
  • Dependency Array: The second argument to useEffect, listing all reactive values (props, state, and derived variables) read inside the effect to tell React when to re-synchronize.
  • Strict Mode Re-synchronization: React development behavior that executes setup, cleanup, and setup on initial mount to verify that effect cleanup routines completely undo setup actions.

Summary

The Lifecycle of a Reactive Effect in React 19

In production applications, understanding the independent lifecycle of reactive effects prevents zombie connections, memory leaks, and out-of-sync external systems. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Core Principles of Effect Synchronization
  1. Think of effects as synchronization cycles, not component lifecycles.
        (a) Components mount, update, and unmount; effects start synchronizing and stop synchronizing.
        (b) An effect may start and stop synchronization dozens of times while its host component remains continuously mounted.
  2. React always runs cleanup before re-setup when dependencies change.
        (a) Before connecting to the new dependency, React calls the cleanup function from the previous render.
        (b) Closure capture ensures the cleanup function accesses the exact props and state from the render that created it.
  3. Every setup must have a mirror cleanup function that completely reverses it.
        (a) If setup connects, cleanup must disconnect; if setup subscribes, cleanup must unsubscribe.
        (b) Strict Mode in development tests this symmetry by running setup, cleanup, and setup immediately on mount.

➔ NEVER assume an effect only cleans up when the component leaves the screen.

➔ ALWAYS return a cleanup function from effects that open connections, subscriptions, or timers.

➔ IF an effect reads a reactive prop or state variable THEN include it in the dependency array to trigger timely re-synchronization.

DO THIS: Return a mirror cleanup function that reverses setup and cleanly releases external resources.

Resilient Effect Pattern
1function ChatRoom({ roomId }) {
2 useEffect(() => {
3 const connection = createConnection(roomId);
4 connection.connect();
5 return () => {
6 connection.disconnect();
Cleans up old channel before next setup
7 };
8 }, [roomId]);
9 return <h2>Room: #{roomId}</h2>;
10}

DO NOT DO THIS: Never omit cleanup or treat effects as mount-only routines when dependencies change.

Leaky Effect Pattern
1function LeakyChatRoom({ roomId }) {
2 useEffect(() => {
3 const connection = createConnection(roomId);
4 connection.connect();
Leaks old connection when roomId changes
5 }, [roomId]);
Missing cleanup leaves zombie sockets active
6 return <h2>Room: #{roomId}</h2>;
7}

Lecture 39: Extracting and Reusing Stateful Logic with Custom Hooks

Interview Question

CORE

How do you extract and reuse stateful logic between components?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A developer named Marcus builds an editorial newsroom workspace for The National Times website.
  2. Two separate components need network status: a status bar displaying connection health, and a draft button that disables saving when offline.
  3. Marcus copy-pastes identical useState and useEffect blocks into both components, but updating event cleanup in one file leaves the other out of sync.
  4. How do you extract and reuse stateful logic between components?
  5. If you duplicate logic across components, bug fixes drift apart and maintenance costs multiply. If you assume custom hooks share state, you introduce severe data bugs.
  6. Both components call the exact same hook function, yet updating the state in one component never modifies the state of the other.
  7. Today you learn how to extract custom hooks, how React allocates hook memory to individual fiber nodes, and how to share logic cleanly without sharing state.

Component Architecture and the Logic Extraction Divide

In earlier lessons, we learned that React components maintain local state using useState and synchronize with external browser APIs using useEffect (see Lecture 1 and Lecture 28). In an editorial desk, components often need to observe the same external browser condition, such as whether the device is currently online or offline. Developers often assume that because two components need the exact same reactive behavior, they must either copy-paste the code or lift state to a distant parent container.

In plain JavaScript, when two functions need the same calculation, you extract a shared helper function. In React, however, a standard helper function cannot call useState or useEffect. If you copy-paste the hook calls directly into both NetworkStatusBar and SaveDraftButton, both files maintain identical lines of setup, subscription, and cleanup code. Duplicating stateful logic creates state drift: fixing a missing event listener or correcting an event type in one file leaves the second file broken.

Here is the legacy copy-paste duplication pattern showing identical hook boilerplate repeated across components:

Copy-Paste Duplication Pattern
1const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(true);
STATE:
Tracks connectivity locally in component 1
2useEffect(() => {
3 const handle = () => setIsOnline(navigator.onLine);
EFFECT:
Registers online/offline browser listeners
4 window.addEventListener('online', handle);
5 window.addEventListener('offline', handle);
6 return () => {
7 window.removeEventListener('online', handle);
8 window.removeEventListener('offline', handle);
9 };
10}, []);

Look at the code above: to give NetworkStatusBar access to the browser's online status, we had to declare a local state variable and write an effect with two event listeners and two cleanup calls. If another component, such as SaveDraftButton, needs that exact same network status, a developer following this pattern copy-pastes those exact nine lines into the second file. Now your project has eighteen lines of low-level subscription boilerplate across two files. If you ever update the event handler or add a reconnection ping, you must remember to edit both files by hand.

What is a custom hook? In standard JavaScript, an ordinary utility function can compute values, format dates, or transform arrays, but it has no memory and cannot participate in React's component lifecycle. When you write an ordinary function, it executes once and discards all local variables when it returns. A custom hook takes that standard JavaScript function and authorizes it to call other React hooks inside its body. You write a function whose name starts with use, such as function useOnlineStatus() and place useState and useEffect inside it. The custom hook encapsulates the stateful recipe: it tells React how to declare state, how to subscribe to external browser events, and what value to return to the caller. The law of custom hooks is absolute: a custom hook shares the stateful logic and lifecycle recipe, but it never shares state itself; each component calling the hook receives its own completely isolated state cell in memory.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Does a custom hook share state between components? Imagine two pastry chefs in two separate kitchens baking sourdough bread. They both open the exact same cookbook to page forty and follow the exact same recipe. Does that mean they share the same loaf of bread? Of course not. Chef Elena mixes her own flour, water, and yeast in her kitchen bowl. Chef Marcus mixes his own flour, water, and yeast in his kitchen bowl. If Marcus burns his loaf in the oven, Elena's loaf is completely unharmed. This is the difference between sharing a recipe and sharing the food. A custom hook is a recipe for stateful logic. When NetworkStatusBar calls useOnlineStatus(), it bakes its own private component state. When SaveDraftButton calls useOnlineStatus(), it bakes its own private component state. They share the recipe for subscribing to the browser, but their state remains completely independent.
Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example NetworkStatusBar SaveDraftButton

To experience how custom hooks extract stateful logic cleanly while maintaining complete state isolation between components, consider the editorial newsroom workspace on The National Times. The layout EditorialDesk.jsx hosts two distinct user interface widgets:

  1. A live status bar (NetworkStatusBar.jsx) that displays current network connectivity with a colored badge.
  2. A draft saving button (SaveDraftButton.jsx) that disables itself to prevent data loss whenever the internet connection drops.

Before writing any code, examine the final rendered interface we are building. Notice that this visual panel represents the authentic rendered user interface on screen, without code distractions:

Below it sits the editorial draft button, ready to save the reporter's work when online and disable itself when disconnected.

Here is the file layout on disk:

To construct this architecture, we follow a top-down assembly pipeline: we start with the parent workspace container, extract the custom hook, and then build each consumer component:

Step 1
First, we construct the parent container EditorialDesk.jsx

We start our implementation at the top: the parent container EditorialDesk.jsx.

We begin here because the parent establishes the layout of the newsroom desk. Notice that it mounts both child components without passing any network-related state or callbacks:

EditorialDesk.jsx
1export default function EditorialDesk() {
2 const handleSave = () => console.log('Draft saved');
ACTION:
Persists current newsroom article draft
3 return (
4 <main className="desk-layout">
5 <NetworkStatusBar />
MOUNT:
Displays live network connectivity badge
6 <SaveDraftButton onSave={handleSave} />
MOUNT:
Disables save action when network drops
7 </main>
8 );
9}

Look at line 2: const handleSave = () => console.log('Draft saved') The parent declares the action handler that persists the reporter's article draft.

Now look at lines 5 and 6: <NetworkStatusBar /> and <SaveDraftButton onSave={handleSave} /> Notice what is deliberately absent: there is no isOnline state declared in this parent container, and zero network props passed downward.

We could have declared const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(true) right here in EditorialDesk and passed isOnline down to both children. But lifting state to this parent would be a serious architectural flaw. Why? Because every time the device's internet connection flickered, this entire parent container and all its unrelated child views would re-render. By leaving the parent lean, we keep its rendering cost at zero. Each child will subscribe to the network on its own terms.

To recap this first step: the parent provides the structural layout, leaving network synchronization entirely to the child boundaries.

Step 2
Next, we extract the custom hook useOnlineStatus.js

In step 2, we extract the reusable stateful logic into our custom hook: useOnlineStatus.js.

Notice the function name begins with the mandatory lowercase prefix use. This prefix authorizes the function to call React's built-in hooks:

useOnlineStatus.js
1import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
2export function useOnlineStatus() {
3 const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);
STATE:
Local state initialized from browser navigator
4 useEffect(() => {
5 function updateStatus() {
6 setIsOnline(navigator.onLine);
EVENT:
Synchronizes state with native browser network state
7 }
8 window.addEventListener('online', updateStatus);
9 window.addEventListener('offline', updateStatus);

Look at line 3: const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine) We read the browser's native navigator.onLine property to establish our starting state. If the device is connected when the component mounts, isOnline starts as true.

Now examine the useEffect call starting on line 4. Inside the effect, we define a small helper function updateStatus that reads navigator.onLine and passes the fresh boolean to setIsOnline. We attach this helper to two native window events: online and offline. Whenever the operating system detects a network change, the browser dispatches one of these events, and our helper synchronizes our state variable immediately.

Now let us complete the custom hook by adding its cleanup function and returning the boolean state:

11 return () => {
12 window.removeEventListener('online', updateStatus);
CLEANUP:
Detaches listeners on unmount to prevent leaks
13 window.removeEventListener('offline', updateStatus);
14 };
15 }, []);
16 return isOnline;
RETURN:
Exposes current boolean status to calling component
17}

Look at lines 11 to 14: the effect returns a cleanup callback that removes both event listeners from the window object. This cleanup callback is essential. Without it, every time a component calling this hook unmounted, its event listeners would remain attached to the global window, leaking memory and executing stale setters in the background.

Finally, look at line 16: return isOnline Notice that we return only the boolean value, not the setter setIsOnline. The custom hook manages its own state updates internally in response to browser events. Components that consume this hook need to know whether the network is active, but they have no business manually overriding that status.

To recap this step: the custom hook encapsulates state declaration, event subscription, and cleanup into a single reusable function returning a clean boolean.

Step 3
Then, we build the status indicator NetworkStatusBar.jsx

In step 3, we build our first consumer component: NetworkStatusBar.jsx.

This child component renders a visual badge in the newsroom header, displaying a green indicator when online and a red warning when disconnected:

NetworkStatusBar.jsx
1import { useOnlineStatus } from '../hooks/useOnlineStatus.js';
2export default function NetworkStatusBar() {
3 const isOnline = useOnlineStatus();
HOOK:
Subscribes to network status using custom hook
4 return (
5 <aside className={isOnline ? 'status-online' : 'status-offline'}>
6 <span className="indicator-dot" />
UI:
Visual colored dot reflecting connectivity
7 {isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Disconnected'}
8 </aside>
9 );
10}

Look at line 3: const isOnline = useOnlineStatus() With this single line, NetworkStatusBar gains full access to live network connectivity.

Notice what is missing from this file: there is no useState declaration, no useEffect hook, no window.addEventListener calls, and no cleanup logic. All of that low-level subscription plumbing is neatly tucked away inside useOnlineStatus.

When NetworkStatusBar mounts, React executes useOnlineStatus() and assigns a private state cell to this component. If the network drops, the hook calls its internal setter, and React re-renders only NetworkStatusBar. The badge updates its CSS class and text immediately.

To recap this step: calling a custom hook lets a component consume complex stateful logic in a single, readable line of code.

Step 4
Finally, we build the action control SaveDraftButton.jsx

In step 4, we build our second consumer component: SaveDraftButton.jsx.

This component renders the button editors click to save their news articles. When the internet connection drops, the button must disable itself so reporters do not submit work into a void:

SaveDraftButton.jsx
1import { useOnlineStatus } from '../hooks/useOnlineStatus.js';
2export default function SaveDraftButton({ onSave }) {
3 const isOnline = useOnlineStatus();
HOOK:
Allocates independent hook cell on this component's fiber
4 return (
5 <button onClick={onSave} disabled={!isOnline} className="save-btn">
6 {isOnline ? 'Save Draft' : 'Reconnecting...'}
UI:
Dynamic label and disabled state when offline
7 </button>
8 );
9}

Look at line 3: const isOnline = useOnlineStatus() Notice that SaveDraftButton calls the exact same custom hook that NetworkStatusBar called in step 3.

Now look at line 5: disabled={!isOnline}. When isOnline is false, the browser natively disables the button, preventing click events and showing a dimmed visual style. The button text also switches dynamically from "Save Draft" to "Reconnecting...".

Look at the button click handler on line 5: onClick={onSave}.

Where does onSave come from? Look back at Step 1 in EditorialDesk.jsx. The parent declared const handleSave = () => console.log('Draft saved') and then rendered: <SaveDraftButton onSave={handleSave} />

Notice what happened: the parent handed its private handler function handleSave to the child under the prop name onSave. SaveDraftButton does not own the saving logic or article content, and it does not know where the draft is stored. It only holds a telephone line called onSave.

When the reporter clicks the button, the native browser onClick fires and calls onSave(). Because onSave points directly to handleSave, that call immediately executes handleSave() back in EditorialDesk.

This is standard inverse data flow: data flows down through props (disabled={!isOnline}), and user actions flow up through callbacks (onSave).

Here is the central lesson: even though SaveDraftButton and NetworkStatusBar call the exact same hook, their state is completely independent. Calling useOnlineStatus() twice creates two separate state variables in React's memory. If you unmount NetworkStatusBar, SaveDraftButton continues to function with zero disruption.

To recap this step: multiple components can call the same custom hook to reuse its logic, while each component retains its own isolated state.

Lessons from the Experiment: Naive Expectation vs Reality

When developers first encounter custom hooks, their naive expectation is that calling a custom hook acts like a global store or shared singleton, connecting all calling components to a single shared state variable. This naive expectation leads to deep confusion when an update in one component fails to trigger re-renders in other components calling the same hook.

In our newsroom experiment, both NetworkStatusBar and SaveDraftButton called useOnlineStatus(). When the browser fired an online event, both components updated simultaneously. However, they did not update because they shared state. They updated because each component had its own independent isOnline state variable, and both happened to receive the same external browser event at the exact same millisecond. Conflating shared logic with shared state causes developers to create buggy custom hooks when managing user-driven state like form inputs or modal toggles.

To inspect how responsibilities divide across files, examine the component relationship architecture:

EditorialDesk

The parent container defines the newsroom workspace layout. Notice it passes zero network props downward to either child. Why? Because lifting network state into the parent would cause the entire container to re-render on every connection flicker, churning child components unnecessarily.

NetworkStatusBar

The first consumer component. It calls useOnlineStatus() to allocate its own private reactive state cell. When the network drops, React re-renders only this component, updating the status badge from green to red without touching the rest of the page.

SaveDraftButtononSave={handleSave}

The second consumer component. It calls the exact same useOnlineStatus() hook. React allocates a second, completely separate state cell on this button's fiber node. It disables itself when offline to protect editors from lost drafts.

Now review the architecture audit table comparing the copy-paste approach against custom hook extraction:

The Fiber Node Memory Model: Why Custom Hooks Do Not Share State

To truly understand why custom hooks do not share state, you must look at where React stores state in memory. In plain JavaScript, if two modules import a shared variable from a file, both modules read and write to that exact same variable in memory. Developers often assume that because a custom hook is declared in a single file (useOnlineStatus.js), the state inside that file behaves like a module-level variable.

In React, a custom hook owns zero memory of its own. A custom hook is not a component, not a class, and not an actor. It is simply a JavaScript function that executes inside the context of whichever component called it. When a component calls useOnlineStatus(), React looks at the fiber node currently being processed on the work loop. Calling useState inside a custom hook tells React: "allocate a new state cell on the currently executing fiber node." If two components call the hook, React creates two separate state cells on two separate fiber nodes.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Where does custom hook state actually live? Imagine a carpenter who owns a set of measuring tools. When the carpenter works on house number one, they use their ruler to measure a wooden door. When the carpenter works on house number two, they use the exact same ruler to measure a wooden window. Does house number two have a door because the carpenter used the same ruler? No. The ruler does not own the wood; the house owns the wood. The ruler is simply the tool used to shape it. A custom hook is like that ruler. The hook does not own any component state. When NetworkStatusBar calls the hook, React allocates the state inside NetworkStatusBar's fiber node. When SaveDraftButton calls the hook, React allocates the state inside SaveDraftButton's fiber node. The state lives inside the component, never inside the hook.

The use Prefix Convention and Linter Contract

In standard JavaScript, you can name a function anything you want: getOnlineStatus, calculateTotal, or syncNetwork. In React, however, any function that calls other React hooks must start with the lowercase prefix use, written in camelCase (such as useOnlineStatus or useWindowSize). Developers who name a custom hook with a standard prefix like getOnlineStatus encounter linter errors or mysterious runtime bugs.

React hooks rely on an internal invariant: hooks must be called in the exact same order on every single render. You cannot call hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. Because React cannot inspect the internal body of every third-party function at compile time, it relies on the use prefix as an explicit syntactic contract. The use prefix signals to the React linter that this function contains hook calls and must obey the Rules of Hooks. If you name it getOnlineStatus, the linter assumes it is an ordinary function, allowing developers to call it inside an if statement and corrupting React's internal hook linked list.

When should a function be a custom hook versus an ordinary utility function? The rule is straightforward: (a) if the function calls at least one React hook (useState, useEffect, useContext, useRef), it must be named with the use prefix and treated as a custom hook; (b) if the function performs pure data transformation, string formatting, or mathematical calculation without calling any React hooks, it should be an ordinary utility function without the use prefix. Naming a pure function with use restricts it unnecessarily, preventing it from being called conditionally or inside loops.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked how custom hooks work under the hood, never say "they share state between components." State clearly that custom hooks share stateful logic, not state. Explain that hooks are pure syntactic composition: calling a custom hook executes its internal useState and useEffect calls directly against the calling component's current fiber node. Each component gets its own independent state cell in the fiber linked list. If you need to share state itself, you must either lift state to a common ancestor or use React Context.

Where you will meet this

  • Network connectivity monitoring (useOnlineStatus): Subscribing to browser online and offline events to display status banners and disable mutation buttons in offline-resilient applications.
  • Window dimensions and responsive breakpoints (useWindowSize): Listening to browser resize events to dynamically switch between mobile drawer navigation and desktop sidebar layouts.
  • Form input controllers and validation (useFormField): Encapsulating value state, change handlers, validation rules, and error messages across recurring input fields.
  • LocalStorage synchronization (useLocalStorage): Syncing a reactive state variable with browser storage so user preferences like dark mode or collapsed sidebars persist across page reloads.

Glossary

  • Custom Hook: A JavaScript function whose name starts with use that can call other React hooks, encapsulating reusable stateful logic and lifecycle synchronization for components.
  • Stateful Logic: The instructions, event subscriptions, and effect lifecycles that govern how state is declared, updated, and synchronized over time.
  • Fiber Hook Cell: An internal JavaScript object within a component fiber's linked list that stores the state value, memoized calculation, or effect cleanup for a specific hook call.
  • Rules of Hooks: The fundamental constraints governing hook execution: hooks must only be called at the top level of React function components or custom hooks, and never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions.
  • State Isolation: The core React guarantee that state declared by a hook belongs exclusively to the component instance that invoked it, remaining completely independent of other components calling the same hook.
  • Lifecycle Synchronization: The process of keeping React component state aligned with an external system, such as browser window events, network sockets, or hardware sensors, using effects.

Summary

Extracting and Reusing Stateful Logic with Custom Hooks

In production React applications, custom hooks allow developers to extract complex stateful logic and lifecycle subscriptions into clean, reusable modules without sharing state. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Core Principles of Custom Hook Architecture
  1. Custom hooks share stateful logic, never state itself.
        (a) Each component that calls a custom hook receives its own independent state storage on its private fiber node.
        (b) Two components calling the same hook update independently unless both subscribe to the exact same external browser event.
  2. Hook names must always begin with the lowercase prefix use.
        (a) The use prefix informs React and linting tools that the function contains hook calls and must follow the Rules of Hooks.
        (b) Functions that do not call React hooks must not use the use prefix, allowing them to be called conditionally.
  3. Use custom hooks to eliminate copy-pasted effect boilerplate.
        (a) Encapsulate browser event subscriptions, timers, and storage listeners inside a single custom hook.
        (b) Keep component files focused on visual presentation rather than low-level event listener wiring.

➔ NEVER assume that calling a custom hook in two components shares a single state variable between them.

➔ ALWAYS name custom hooks starting with use so the linter can enforce the Rules of Hooks.

➔ IF a function does not call any React hooks THEN name it as a standard utility function without the use prefix.

DO THIS: Extract stateful logic into a custom hook and let each component call it independently.

useOnlineStatus.js
1export function useOnlineStatus() {
2 const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);
3 useEffect(() => {
4 const handle = () => setIsOnline(navigator.onLine);
5 window.addEventListener('online', handle);
6 window.addEventListener('offline', handle);
7 return () => {
8 window.removeEventListener('online', handle);
9 window.removeEventListener('offline', handle);
10 };
11 }, []);
12 return isOnline;
13}

DO NOT DO THIS: Never copy-paste identical useState and useEffect subscription blocks across multiple components.

Copy-Pasted Hook Anti-Pattern

2 const [isOnline, setIsOnline] = useState(true);
3 useEffect(() => {
4 const handle = () => setIsOnline(navigator.onLine);
5 window.addEventListener('online', handle);
6 return () => window.removeEventListener('online', handle);
7 }, []);
8 return <span>{isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Offline'}</span>;
9}

Lecture 40: Forms: Controlled State versus Uncontrolled FormData

Interview Question

MORE

Should a form use controlled state or uncontrolled FormData, and how do you choose?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. A developer named Elena builds an article correction form for The National Times website.
  2. The form collects a reader's name, email, and correction commentary across several text fields.
  3. Elena binds every single input with value and onChange, but typing lags noticeably on mobile devices.
  4. Should a form use controlled state or uncontrolled FormData, and how do you choose?
  5. If you control every input, you introduce typing lag and heavy state boilerplate. If you leave everything uncontrolled, you lose real-time validation.
  6. Both approaches collect user data. But one forces React to re-render on every keypress, while the other leaves text in the browser until submit.
  7. Today you learn the mechanical differences, runtime performance trade-offs, and the senior decision matrix for choosing between them.

Component Architecture and the State Ownership Divide

In earlier lessons, we learned that React components maintain local reactive memory using the useState hook (see Lecture 1). When you build an interactive form, your immediate instinct is to store every character the user types inside a component state variable. Developers often assume that controlling every input is the only way to manage form data in React.

What is a controlled input? React draws a clear line between two kinds of inputs. One is the controlled input, governed by React. The other is the uncontrolled input, governed by the browser. In normal HTML, an input controls itself. When you type a letter, the browser stores that letter directly in its native C++ buffer and paints it on screen. No JavaScript is involved. When you leave an input like that, React calls it an uncontrolled input. In a controlled input, you take that power away from the browser. You write <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} /> The input is now locked. It can only display whatever the state variable holds. React dictates every single character shown on screen.

Here is the minimal code comparison between the two approaches:

Controlled vs Uncontrolled
1<input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
1. Controlled: React dictates value via STATE
2<input name="contributor" defaultValue="Elena Rostova" />
2. Uncontrolled: Browser holds text in native DOM

In a controlled input, you bind the value attribute to a state variable. You also attach an onChange listener to update that state on every keystroke. Now imagine typing the word hello into that field one letter at a time. Each keypress dispatches an event and updates state. React wakes the fiber reconciler. It re-runs the component function and recomputes the virtual DOM. Finally, it writes the updated string back into the DOM node. The component re-renders on every keystroke. The CPU recalculates the entire component tree five times just to type a five-letter word.

⚡ IN THE WILD

What does controlling an input really mean? Imagine typing your name into a physical guestbook. In plain HTML, the pen writes directly onto paper, and the paper holds the ink. In a controlled input, you never write on the paper directly. Instead, you whisper each letter to an assistant named React. React writes the letter in its private notebook, erases the paper, and rewrites the letter for you. Type five letters, and React rewrites the paper five times. This gives React complete control over the paper. But whispering and rewriting on every keypress creates unnecessary overhead. In most forms, you only care about the finished name on submit. An uncontrolled input lets the browser hold the ink until you hand in the book.
Case Study

  1. A live headline search input (LiveSearchInput.jsx) that filters published stories in real time as the editor types.
  2. An article correction form (ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx) where readers submit contributor feedback only when clicking submit.

Look at line 3: const [query, setQuery] = useState('') We declare state here because search filtering requires real-time synchronization on every keystroke.

Now look at line 6: <LiveSearchInput query={query} onChange={setQuery} /> We have not coded LiveSearchInput yet. But right here in the parent, we establish its contract. The parent owns the search text, and passes a callback so the child can report keypresses. We will build that child next in step 2.

Now look at line 7: <ArticleCorrectionForm />. Notice that it takes zero props, zero state, and zero callbacks. We could have declared state variables for the contributor name and commentary right here in FeedbackPortal. But that would be a serious design mistake. Why? Because every single letter typed into the commentary box would force this entire parent container and the child search input to re-render repeatedly. By giving it zero props, we isolate it completely. We will build that form in steps 3 and 4.

To recap this first step: the parent holds the shared state that child components need to coordinate, and leaves independent forms completely isolated.

Step 2
Next, we build the controlled child LiveSearchInput.jsx

In step 2, we fulfill the contract established by the parent: we build LiveSearchInput.jsx.

This child component is responsible for the live search pill at the top of the portal:

LiveSearchInput.jsx
1export default function LiveSearchInput({ query, onChange }) {
DATA FLOW:
Receives active search query and updater callback from parent
2 return (
3 <input
4 value={query}
CODE LOGIC:
Locks displayed text strictly to React state as single source of truth
5 onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
DATA FLOW:
Forwards typed character upward on every keystroke to update state
6 placeholder="Filter by headline..."
7 className="search-input"
8 />
9 );
10}

Notice the function parameters: we destructure { query, onChange } directly from props. That matches the contract we wrote in step 1. LiveSearchInput owns zero local state. It relies entirely on its parent to provide the search text and the function to update it.

Look at the input event handler on line 5: onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}

Where does onChange come from? Look back at Step 1 in FeedbackPortal.jsx. The parent declared const [query, setQuery] = useState('') and then rendered: <LiveSearchInput query={query} onChange={setQuery} />

Notice what happened: the parent handed its private updater function setQuery to the child under the prop name onChange. LiveSearchInput does not own state, and it does not know what query is used for. It only holds a telephone line called onChange.

When the editor types a character, the native browser onChange event fires and calls onChange(e.target.value). Because onChange points directly to setQuery, that call immediately executes setQuery(e.target.value) back in FeedbackPortal.

This is standard inverse data flow: data flows down through props (query), and user actions flow up through callbacks (onChange).

What would happen if LiveSearchInput declared its own local useState for the query?

If LiveSearchInput owned the query state locally, the parent FeedbackPortal and the headline news feed would have no way to access the query string without complex ref forwarding or state-lifting hacks. The search input would filter itself in isolation while the article feed remained completely unchanged.

By separating them, LiveSearchInput owns zero local state. It is a pure controlled presenter: given query and onChange, it displays the string and reports keystrokes.

This separation gives you two concrete superpowers:

  1. If tomorrow you replace this text field with a voice-dictation search input, you touch zero lines of filtering logic in the parent.
  2. If you change how the article feed filters stories (such as searching by author instead of headline), you touch zero lines of input code.

To recap this step: data flows down from the parent through query, and user events flow up through onChange.

Step 3
Then, we declare the uncontrolled form ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx

In step 3, we build our second child component: ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx.

Remember how we mounted ArticleCorrectionForm in step 1 without any props? Here is why.

Think about how a reader uses this correction form. They type their name. Then they write a few sentences of feedback. While they are typing, React does not need to know a single letter. We only need that text once: the moment they click submit:

ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx
1export default function ArticleCorrectionForm() {
2 async function handleSubmit(formData) {

Receives native FormData dictionary containing all named inputs on submit
3 const contributor = formData.get('contributor');
CODE LOGIC:
Reads contributor name from native buffer with zero re-renders
4 const commentary = formData.get('commentary');

5 console.log('Correction submitted:', { contributor, commentary });

10 <textarea name="commentary" placeholder="Describe the correction..." />

Look closely at the markup inside the form. Notice what is missing: there is no value prop, no onChange listener, and not a single useState hook anywhere in this file.

Instead, notice defaultValue="Elena Rostova". That sets an initial starting string when the input first mounts. From that moment on, the browser's native C++ engine takes over. It stores every typed character directly in its own buffer. When a reader types three paragraphs of feedback, React does not execute a single line of code. The component never re-renders.

Never forget to include the name attribute on every input. Notice we wrote name="contributor" and name="commentary". Without a name, the browser has no key to associate with the value, and the data will be lost during submission.

Now look at handleSubmit(formData) at the top of the component. When submission happens, React 19 hands us a native FormData instance containing all named fields. We simply call formData.get('contributor') and formData.get('commentary') to extract the values.

Notice the contrast with step 2: in step 2, React synchronized every keystroke in real time. Here in step 3, React stays completely idle while the user types. It only harvests the data at the final moment of submission.

Step 4
Finally, we seal the form with native action submission

In step 4, we complete ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx by adding the submit button and closing the form tag:

ArticleCorrectionForm.jsx (continued)
11 <button type="submit">Submit Correction</button>

Fires submit event to trigger native form action pipeline
12 </form>
CODE LOGIC:
Form boundary isolates input typing from parent re-renders

14}

Notice the submit button on line 11. When the user clicks this button or presses Enter inside an input field, the browser fires a native submit event on the enclosing <form>.

In classic React, you had to attach an onSubmit handler to the form. You had to call e.preventDefault() to stop the page from reloading. Then you had to gather your form data manually.

Notice what we wrote on line 8 instead: <form action={handleSubmit}>. In React 19, passing an async function to action tells React to intercept the submission automatically. React prevents the page reload. It gathers the named inputs into FormData. Then it runs handleSubmit inside a background transition, so the rest of the page stays responsive.

The <form> boundary seals this entire workflow. It is completely self-contained. It collects its own data, triggers its own action, and never forces the parent container FeedbackPortal to re-render.

Let us recap the senior rule. Use controlled state when you need immediate, per-keystroke synchronization, such as live search filtering. Use uncontrolled FormData when you only care about the values at the moment of submission.

Lessons from the Experiment: Naive Expectation vs Reality

Developers instinctively assume that all form inputs in React must be wired to local useState hooks to function properly. This naive expectation leads to dozens of redundant state declarations, verbose event handlers, and severe typing lag on complex pages.

In our experiment, the search input needed controlled state. The headline list must filter in real time on every keystroke. The correction form was different. We only needed its data when the user clicked submit. If we controlled the correction form, React would re-render the entire portal on every single keypress. That extra work provides zero benefit to the user.

To see the architectural hierarchy and component relationships at a glance, examine how each component functions in direct relation to the others:

FeedbackPortal

The parent component orchestrates the overall portal layout. It owns the live search state. Also, it actively provides two things: the state (props) and updater functions downward to LiveSearchInput. Notice it deliberately passes zero props to ArticleCorrectionForm. Why? To isolate the parent from typing re-renders.

LiveSearchInputquery={query} onChange={setQuery}

This is the controlled child component. It receives two things from the parent: the state (query) and the updater function (onChange). Notice it locks the input's displayed value directly to React state. Why? To filter published headlines in real time on every single keystroke.

ArticleCorrectionForm

This is the uncontrolled child component. Notice it receives zero props and zero callbacks from the parent. The browser stores all text in its native C++ buffer. When does React read the data? Only once, on submit, using FormData. This keeps typing at 60 FPS with zero parent re-renders.

The Per-Keystroke Latency Bottleneck

On a high-performance desktop computer, running a small component function five times while typing a word takes less than a millisecond. On a budget smartphone with a busy CPU, re-rendering a large component tree on every keystroke causes frame drops and sluggish typing latency. Controlling every input indiscriminately degrades user experience on low-end devices.

When an input is controlled, typing a character triggers a state update. That schedules work on the React fiber work loop. Now imagine the component tree contains fifty child components, complex charts, or heavy layout elements. React must reconcile that entire tree before the browser paints the newly typed character. If reconciliation takes more than 16 milliseconds, the frame drops. The user experiences input lag. Typed characters appear seconds after their fingers leave the glass.

Uncontrolled inputs bypass the React work loop completely while typing. The native browser engine handles character insertion in compiled C++. Typing stays at a solid 60 frames per second, no matter how large the React application is. You pay zero rendering cost until the user clicks submit.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does typing lag on mobile devices? Imagine typing a message on your smartphone. You tap five keys quickly, but the letters appear on screen with a sluggish delay. Why? Because every single keypress forced React to re-render the entire page. The computer was busy recalculating layout trees, re-rendering sidebars, and diffing virtual DOM trees instead of simply painting the letter you typed. This is the input latency bottleneck of over-controlled forms. Uncontrolled inputs eliminate this lag completely. The browser handles text entry in native C++, and React stays completely idle until the user taps submit.

The Senior Engineering Decision Matrix

Senior engineers do not choose between controlled and uncontrolled inputs based on habit or dogma. They evaluate the concrete functional requirements of the specific form control.

When should you choose controlled inputs? Choose controlled inputs when you need immediate, synchronous access to the field's value while the user is actively typing. Specifically:

  • Live Search Filtering: Query strings that filter lists, tables, or autocomplete dropdowns on every keystroke.
  • Input Masking and Formatting: Fields requiring immediate character formatting, such as phone numbers, dates, or currency strings.
  • Dynamic Field Dependencies: Scenarios where typing in one field dynamically shows, hides, or disables another field.
  • Instant Character Counters: Live feedback widgets such as password strength meters or remaining character counters.

When should you choose uncontrolled inputs with FormData? Choose uncontrolled inputs when you only need the field values at the moment of submission. Specifically:

  • Standard Data Collection Forms: Contact forms, feedback submissions, user registration, and account profiles.
  • Large Multi-Field Forms: Forms with dozens of fields where per-keystroke re-rendering causes performance bottlenecks.
  • Long-Form Text Editing: Article authoring, commentary, and description fields where users type long paragraphs of text.
  • React 19 Form Actions: Workflows leveraging modern form actions, automatic resets, and progressive enhancement.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked whether forms should be controlled or uncontrolled, never say "always control everything." Explain the architectural trade-off. Controlled inputs provide instant real-time synchronization, but they cause per-keystroke re-renders and boilerplate state. Uncontrolled inputs with FormData isolate typing from the React work loop. They deliver maximum performance and clean code for standard submit-only workflows.

Where you will meet this

  • Editorial correction forms: Collecting contributor names, emails, and multi-line correction notes using uncontrolled FormData for zero-lag text editing.
  • Live article search filters: Synchronizing search query strings with controlled state to filter published headlines in real time as the editor types.
  • Subscriber checkout billing: Formatting credit card expiration dates and security codes with controlled input masks to guarantee valid character formatting.
  • User settings and profile updates: Harvesting user preferences, notification toggles, and biographical text using native FormData on submit without local state hooks.

Glossary

  • Controlled Input: An input element whose displayed value is bound to a React state variable and updated synchronously via an onChange handler on every keystroke.
  • Uncontrolled Input: An input element that stores its value in the native browser buffer, accessed on demand via a ref or harvested on form submission through FormData.
  • FormData: A native browser object providing a key-value representation of form fields, populated automatically from named inputs upon form submission.
  • Single Source of Truth: The design principle where application state lives in exactly one place (React state for controlled inputs, or the DOM for uncontrolled inputs).
  • Input Latency: The delay between a physical keystroke on the keyboard and the visual rendering of the corresponding character on screen, exacerbated by per-keystroke component re-renders.
  • DefaultValue: The initial value supplied to an uncontrolled input at mount time, allowing the browser to manage subsequent edits without React state intervention.

Summary

Controlled State versus Uncontrolled FormData in React Forms

In production applications, choosing between controlled state and uncontrolled FormData defines both developer ergonomics and runtime rendering performance. Here is your streetwise review.

❒ Core Principles of Form State Architecture
  1. Use uncontrolled inputs with FormData as your default strategy for standard submit-only forms.
        (a) Storing text in the native browser buffer eliminates per-keystroke re-renders and state boilerplate.
        (b) Named inputs are harvested automatically into a native FormData dictionary on submit.
  2. Reserve controlled inputs for fields that require real-time synchronization during typing.
        (a) Live search filters, character counters, and input formatting masks require immediate access to every keystroke.
        (b) Binding value and onChange forces React to re-render on every keypress, creating input latency on large trees.
  3. Protect mobile performance by avoiding over-controlled forms.
        (a) Controlling dozens of fields in a single component causes cumulative layout recalculation and typing lag.
        (b) Keep inputs uncontrolled unless a specific real-time feature demands per-keystroke state.

➔ NEVER control an input if you only read its value when the user clicks submit.

➔ ALWAYS supply a name attribute to uncontrolled inputs so FormData can harvest them.

➔ IF you need real-time validation or live search filtering THEN bind value and onChange with controlled state.

DO THIS: Use uncontrolled inputs with name attributes and harvest values via FormData on submit.
